query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ∼100 nm-thick, conformal Ti barrier layer to all W surfaces BEFORE Cu infiltration will suppress W–Cu phase separation and interfacial Kirkendall voiding, so that after thermal cycling and fusion-relevant ion irradiation the through-thickness thermal conductivity of the coated W-Cu composite is ≥15 % higher than that of an otherwise identical, uncoated composite.
generation.material_initial_state: Porous W preform (35–60 vol % solid fraction, ligament/powder size 5–50 µm) subsequently infiltrated with high-purity Cu to give a conventional W–Cu composite joint material.
generation.intervention: Room-temperature physical vapour deposition of a continuous 100 ± 30 nm Ti film on all exposed W ligament or particle surfaces prior to Cu infiltration; no other chemistry or processing changed.
generation.conditions: Processing: vacuum PVD at <200 °C, followed by standard melt infiltration of Cu at 1250 ± 50 °C for ≤30 min in inert atmosphere.  Service: heat-flux cycles between 25 °C and 600 °C plus 1–3 dpa 1 MeV Cu-ion irradiation at 300 °C (representative of divertor joint exposure).
generation.structural_mediator: During infiltration Ti reacts with Cu to form a nanometric, coherent (Ti,Cu) intermetallic layer and sparse TiC/TiO nanoscale dispersoids that pin the W/Cu interface.
generation.mechanism: 1. The Ti nanolayer lowers the W/Cu interfacial energy and provides a fast short-circuit path for bidirectional diffusion, minimising the Cu↔W diffusivity mismatch that drives Kirkendall porosity.  2. Ti scavenges residual O, forming stable TiO/TiC particles that inhibit gas-bubble nucleation under irradiation.  3. The resulting void-free, coherent interface maintains metallic continuity, raising effective thermal contact conductance.
generation.predicted_outcome: After 1000 thermal cycles and 3 dpa ion irradiation, laser-flash measurements will show the coated composite retains ≥220 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ cross-plane thermal conductivity, at least 15–25 % higher than the uncoated control, which will fall below 190 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ due to interfacial voiding.
generation.baseline: Uncoated W–Cu composite processed identically but without the Ti deposition; expected to develop interfacial voids and >20 % drop in thermal conductivity under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: Valid for W volume fractions 30–70 %, Ti layer 50–300 nm, infiltration temperatures 1150–1300 °C, and service temperatures ≤700 °C.  Outside these ranges (e.g., Ti layer ≥500 nm or service T > 900 °C) excessive intermetallic growth may degrade conductivity.
generation.uncertainty: No direct data yet link such thin Ti layers to long-term irradiation response in W–Cu; magnitude of conductivity benefit (15–25 %) is estimated from interfacial-resistance models and may be over- or under-predicted.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two batches of W-Cu composites with and without the Ti pre-coat, identical in all other respects. Subject matched specimens to: (a) 1000 thermal cycles 25↔600 °C in flowing He; (b) 1 MeV Cu-ion irradiation to 3 dpa at 300 °C. Then measure cross-plane thermal conductivity and image W/Cu interfaces by TEM and 3-D tomography.
measurements: Through-thickness thermal conductivity (laser-flash) before and after exposure
Void density and size distribution at W/Cu interfaces (FIB-SEM tomography)
Phase and thickness of interfacial layers (TEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-coated specimens do NOT show (i) ≥15 % higher post-exposure thermal conductivity than uncoated controls AND (ii) ≥50 % lower interfacial void volume fraction, the hypothesis is falsified.
